claim: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration is the second most common type of early-onset dementia under the age of 65 years.
source: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration is the second most common type of early-onset dementia under the age of 65 years (Harvey et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harvey et al., 2003

claim: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is the most common subtype of frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: Its most common subtype, behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), is characterized by detrimental changes in personality and behavior (Pressman and Miller, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pressman and Miller, 2014

claim: bvFTD is characterized by detrimental changes in personality and behavior.
source: Its most common subtype, behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), is characterized by detrimental changes in personality and behavior (Pressman and Miller, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pressman and Miller, 2014

claim: bvFTD patients can display both apathy and disinhibition.
source: Patients can display both apathy and disinhibition, often combined with a lack of insight, and executive and socioemotional deficits (Schroeter et al., 2011; Schroeter et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schroeter et al., 2011 and 2012

claim: bvFTD patients often have a lack of insight.
source: Patients can display both apathy and disinhibition, often combined with a lack of insight, and executive and socioemotional deficits (Schroeter et al., 2011; Schroeter et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schroeter et al., 2011 and 2012

claim: bvFTD patients have executive and socioemotional deficits.
source: Patients can display both apathy and disinhibition, often combined with a lack of insight, and executive and socioemotional deficits (Schroeter et al., 2011; Schroeter et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schroeter et al., 2011 and 2012

claim: Up to 50% of bvFTD patients are misdiagnosed as having a psychiatric illness rather than a neurodegenerative disease.
source: Despite striking and early symptoms, bvFTD patients are often (i.e. up to 50%) misdiagnosed as having a psychiatric illness rather than a neurodegenerative disease (Woolley et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woolley et al., 2011

claim: Atrophy in frontoinsular areas only occurs in later disease stages of bvFTD.
source: Whereas atrophy in frontoinsular areas only occurs in later disease stages, glucose hypometabolism in frontal, anterior cingulate, and anterior temporal regions visible with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) is already detectable from an early stage onwards (Bang et al., 2015; Diehl-Schmid et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bang et al., 2015 and Diehl-Schmid et al., 2007

claim: Glucose hypometabolism in frontal, anterior cingulate, and anterior temporal regions is detectable from an early stage onwards in bvFTD.
source: Whereas atrophy in frontoinsular areas only occurs in later disease stages, glucose hypometabolism in frontal, anterior cingulate, and anterior temporal regions visible with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) is already detectable from an early stage onwards (Bang et al., 2015; Diehl-Schmid et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bang et al., 2015 and Diehl-Schmid et al., 2007

claim: fALFF is a resting-state functional MRI derived measure with good test-retest reliability.
source: The fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) is a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) derived measure with good test–retest reliability that closely correlates with FDG-PET (Aiello et al., 2015; Holiga et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aiello et al., 2015; Holiga et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2022

claim: fALFF closely correlates with FDG-PET.
source: The fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) is a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) derived measure with good test–retest reliability that closely correlates with FDG-PET (Aiello et al., 2015; Holiga et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aiello et al., 2015; Holiga et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2022

claim: In FTD patients, fALFF was reduced in inferior parietal, frontal lobes, and posterior cingulate cortex.
source: In frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patients, fALFF was reduced in inferior parietal, frontal lobes, and posterior cingulate cortex and holds great potential as MRI biomarker (Premi et al., 2014; Borroni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Premi et al., 2014 and Borroni et al., 2018

claim: fALFF holds great potential as MRI biomarker in FTD.
source: In frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patients, fALFF was reduced in inferior parietal, frontal lobes, and posterior cingulate cortex and holds great potential as MRI biomarker (Premi et al., 2014; Borroni et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Premi et al., 2014 and Borroni et al., 2018

claim: Low local fALFF activity in the left insula was linked to symptom deterioration in FTD.
source: Low local fALFF activity in the left insula was linked to symptom deterioration (Day et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Day et al., 2013

claim: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration can be differentiated into three different subtypes based on abnormal protein deposition: tau, TDP-43, and FET.
source: On a molecular level, frontotemporal lobar degeneration can be differentiated into three different subtypes based on abnormal protein deposition: tau (tau protein), transactive response DNA-binding protein with molecular weight 43 kDa (TDP-43), and FET (fused-in-sarcoma [FUS] and Ewing sarcoma [EWS] proteins, and TATA-binding protein-associated factor 15 [TAF15]) (Bang et al., 2015; Haass and Neumann, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bang et al., 2015 and Haass and Neumann, 2016

claim: Tau and TDP pathologies each occur in half of the bvFTD patients.
source: Whereas tau and TDP pathologies each occur in half of the bvFTD patients, FUS pathology is very rare (Whitwell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitwell et al., 2011

claim: FUS pathology is very rare in bvFTD patients.
source: Whereas tau and TDP pathologies each occur in half of the bvFTD patients, FUS pathology is very rare (Whitwell et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitwell et al., 2011

claim: Tau can cause presynaptic dysfunction prior to loss of function or cell death.
source: For example, tau can cause presynaptic dysfunction prior to loss of function or cell death (Zhou et al., 2017), whereas overexpression of TDP-43 leads to impairment of presynaptic integrity (Heyburn and Moussa, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2017

claim: Overexpression of TDP-43 leads to impairment of presynaptic integrity.
source: For example, tau can cause presynaptic dysfunction prior to loss of function or cell death (Zhou et al., 2017), whereas overexpression of TDP-43 leads to impairment of presynaptic integrity (Heyburn and Moussa, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heyburn and Moussa, 2016

claim: Neuronal connectivity plays a key role in the spread of pathology as it is thought to transmit along neural networks.
source: Neuronal connectivity plays a key role in the spread of pathology as it is thought to transmit along neural networks.
evidence: Supported by established scientific understanding of disease propagation

claim: There is an association between tau levels and functional connectivity in functionally connected brain regions across normal aging and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Supporting the notion, previous studies also found an association between tau levels and functional connectivity in functionally connected brain regions, for example across normal aging and Alzheimer's disease (Franzmeier et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Franzmeier et al., 2019

claim: Dopaminergic, serotonergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission is affected in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: Thereby, dopaminergic, serotonergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission is affected.
evidence: Inferred from the context of neuronal connectivity and pathology spread discussion

claim: There is a deficit of neurons and receptors in dopaminergic, serotonergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurotransmitter systems in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: More specifically, current research indicates a deficit of neurons and receptors in these neurotransmitter systems (Hock and Polymenidou, 2016; Huey et al., 2006; Murley and Rowe, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hock and Polymenidou, 2016; Huey et al., 2006; Murley and Rowe, 2018

claim: GABAergic deficits have been associated with disinhibition in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: For example, whereas GABAergic deficits have been associated with disinhibition, increased dopaminergic neurotransmission and altered serotonergic modulation of dopaminergic neurotransmission have been associated with agitated and aggressive behavior (Engelborghs et al., 2008; Murley et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engelborghs et al., 2008 and Murley et al., 2020

claim: Increased dopaminergic neurotransmission has been associated with agitated and aggressive behavior in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: For example, whereas GABAergic deficits have been associated with disinhibition, increased dopaminergic neurotransmission and altered serotonergic modulation of dopaminergic neurotransmission have been associated with agitated and aggressive behavior (Engelborghs et al., 2008; Murley et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engelborghs et al., 2008 and Murley et al., 2020

claim: Altered serotonergic modulation of dopaminergic neurotransmission has been associated with agitated and aggressive behavior in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: For example, whereas GABAergic deficits have been associated with disinhibition, increased dopaminergic neurotransmission and altered serotonergic modulation of dopaminergic neurotransmission have been associated with agitated and aggressive behavior (Engelborghs et al., 2008; Murley et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engelborghs et al., 2008 and Murley et al., 2020

claim: Apathy is related to glucose hypometabolism in the ventral tegmental area in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
source: Another study related apathy to glucose hypometabolism in the ventral tegmental area, a hub of the dopaminergic network (Schroeter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schroeter et al., 2011

claim: The ventral tegmental area is a hub of the dopaminergic network.
source: Another study related apathy to glucose hypometabolism in the ventral tegmental area, a hub of the dopaminergic network (Schroeter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by established neuroanatomical knowledge and citation to Schroeter et al., 2011

claim: Neurodegeneration in bvFTD is thought to progress through the salience network.
